## Theorem

Every invertible matrix $A \in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ possesses a logarithm; that is, there exists $B \in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ with $e^B = A$.

## Proof

**Step 1 — Reduction to Jordan blocks.**

Let $A \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$. Over $\mathbb{C}$, $A$ admits a Jordan canonical form: there is an invertible $P$ such that

$$A = P\,J\,P^{-1}, \qquad J = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{r} J_{k_i}(\lambda_i),$$

where each $J_{k_i}(\lambda_i) = \lambda_i I_{k_i} + N_i$ is a Jordan block of size $k_i$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_i$, and $N_i$ is the nilpotent matrix with ones on the superdiagonal ($N_i^{k_i}=0$, $N_i^{k_i-1}\neq 0$).

Since $A$ is invertible, every eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda_i \neq 0$.

If for each block we find a matrix $C_i$ with $e^{C_i} = J_{k_i}(\lambda_i)$, then setting $C = \bigoplus_i C_i$ gives $e^C = J$, and $B := P\,C\,P^{-1}$ satisfies $e^B = A$. So it suffices to log each Jordan block.

**Step 2 — Logarithm of a single Jordan block.**

Fix a block $J_k(\lambda) = \lambda I_k + N$ with $\lambda \neq 0$ and $N^k = 0$. Write

$$J_k(\lambda) = \lambda\!\left(I_k + \tfrac{1}{\lambda}N\right).$$

Since $\lambda \neq 0$ and $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed (every nonzero complex number has a logarithm), choose $\mu \in \mathbb{C}$ with $e^\mu = \lambda$.

Set $X := \tfrac{1}{\lambda}N$. Then $X^k = 0$, so $X$ is nilpotent. Define

$$L(X) := \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \frac{(-1)^{j+1}}{j}\,X^{j}.$$

This is the truncation of the Taylor series $\log(1+t) = \sum_{j\geq 1} \frac{(-1)^{j+1}}{j}t^j$ at degree $k-1$. Because $X^k = 0$, the series for $\log(I_k + X)$ terminates exactly, and the formal identity

$$\exp\!\bigl(L(X)\bigr) = I_k + X$$

holds. (This is the standard formal-power-series identity $\exp(\log(1+t)) = 1+t$ in $\mathbb{C}[[t]]$, evaluated at the nilpotent $X$; all series terminate, so no convergence issues arise.)

Therefore

$$e^{L(X)} = I_k + \tfrac{1}{\lambda}N.$$

**Step 3 — Combine.** Since $\mu I_k$ is a scalar matrix, it commutes with every matrix, in particular with $L(X)$. Hence

$$e^{\mu I_k + L(X)} = e^{\mu I_k}\,e^{L(X)} = e^\mu I_k \cdot \left(I_k + \tfrac{1}{\lambda}N\right) = \lambda\!\left(I_k + \tfrac{1}{\lambda}N\right) = \lambda I_k + N = J_k(\lambda).$$

So $C_i := \mu_i I_{k_i} + L(X_i)$ is a logarithm of the $i$-th Jordan block, with $X_i = N_i/\lambda_i$.

**Step 4 — Assemble.** With $C = \bigoplus_i C_i$ and $B = P C P^{-1}$:

$$e^B = P\,e^C\,P^{-1} = P\,J\,P^{-1} = A.$$

Thus every invertible complex matrix has a (complex) matrix logarithm. $\blacksquare$

**Remark.** The hypothesis of invertibility is necessary: if $e^B = A$ then $\det A = e^{\operatorname{tr} B} \neq 0$, so a non-invertible matrix cannot have a logarithm. Over $\mathbb{C}$, invertibility is also sufficient, as shown above. (Over $\mathbb{R}$ the situation is more delicate — a real invertible matrix has a real logarithm iff each Jordan block associated to a negative real eigenvalue occurs an even number of times — but over $\mathbb{C}$ there is no obstruction.)

### PROOF COMPLETE
